title: Deep Dive: The Frontier-Market Telecom Turnaround Everyone’s Missing
description: Once written off by investors, this frontier-market telco is now posting double-digit growth, expanding digital revenues, and trading at less than 4x EBITDA.
body_html:
I spent a good chunk of my career in the trenches of Latin American telecommunications. I learned how emerging market telcos can be wildly undervalued and how patient investors can profit. Back then, I saw market darlings and market orphans. The darlings got all the love; the orphans were ignored, often due to scary headlines or misunderstood risks.

But guess what?

Some of those “roadkill” orphans turned into multi-baggers once the fog lifted.

Fast forward to today: I’m looking at a telecom company far from Latin America, yet eerily familiar in its underdog vibe. This company operates across frontier markets in Asia and Eastern Europe, not the Andes or the Amazon, but the playbook feels similar. It’s a company that the market left for dead when geopolitics went haywire, yet it’s quietly reinventing itself and cranking out growth.

It reminds me of those overlooked LatAm telcos that eventually proved everyone wrong. And as you know me, I can’t resist a good underdog story in the making.

Want the name and the full deep dive? It’s for paid readers. Since I launched beating the tide, my picks have averaged 21% (128% annualized). Upgrade to get the ticker, the sum of parts model, the key risks, and my game plan for entries and exits.

Table of Contents:

  • Thesis in a Nutshell

  • Company History & Evolution: The Making of an Orphan

  • How VEON Makes Money: Telco 101 Meets Digital 2.0

  • Industry Landscape & Growth Outlook: Frontier Markets, Frontier Opportunities

  • Competitive Position & Differentiation: Local Champion with a Digital Twist

  • Management & Capital Allocation: Skin in the Game and a Plan in Motion

  • Valuation: Sum-of-Parts Tells The True Story

  • Risks and the Variant View

  • What to Watch

  • Final Verdict

Thesis in a Nutshell

After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, about 70% of VEON’s business went to war with itself. VEON did not wait for a miracle. It sold the Russian unit, focused the portfolio, and pushed hard into digital services.

Even though the shares have recovered off its lows, the market still prices it like a problem child. Yet the business is growing. In Q2 2025, revenue rose 5.9% y/y. EBITDA rose 13.2% y/y. The mix keeps improving as higher-margin digital scales.

At today’s price, VEON trades at about 3.8x EV/EBITDA and roughly 5x forward earnings. My base case sum-of-parts says $122 per share. That is +138% upside. My bull case is +$140 as Kyivstar gets closer to a fair mark and more assets get recognized.

I also ran the bear. Assume total devastation in Ukraine and mark Kyivstar at zero. Use depressed 3x EBITDA for the OpCos. Give the towers and digital assets lacklustre values. That math lands at $30 per share, or 41% downside.

As an anchor, if VEON only re-rates to the peer average of about 5.4x EV/EBITDA, the stock screens near $79, about +55% from here. However you slice it, the upside overwhelms the downside.

Catalysts are clear. An end to the war. Ongoing tower monetizations. Rising fintech and digital revenues. Each one helps close the gap. Risks exist: war, currencies and politics. But the margin of safety and the path to value realization make this a bet I like.

Company History & Evolution: The Making of an Orphan

Every comeback story starts with a fall from grace. VEON’s journey began as a high-flying emerging markets telecom empire called VimpelCom. If you’re old enough to remember Telenor’s emerging market ventures or the iconic “Beeline” brand in Russia, you know the pedigree.

VimpelCom was formed in 2009 when Russia’s PJSC VimpelCom and Ukraine’s Kyivstar merged (with backing from Norway’s Telenor and Russia’s Alfa Group) . Over the next decade, the company expanded through acquisitions (from Algeria to Bangladesh) and at one point served over 200 million subscribers in +20 countries . It rebranded to VEON in 2017, trying to shed its pure-telco image and signal a shift toward digital tech .

But then, geopolitics dealt a brutal blow. By 2021, nearly half of VEON’s business was in Russia, and another large chunk in Ukraine. When Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, the company was suddenly split between two warring sides.

As the CEO bluntly put it, “two of our largest markets, 70% of the business, went to war with each other.” VEON’s stock collapsed amid sanctions and chaos, and many investors assumed the company was uninvestable. Major banks dropped coverage, credit agencies withdrew ratings; VEON became a corporate pariah overnight . Talk about a fall from grace.

Here’s where things get interesting: instead of giving up, VEON fought to survive and adapt. Management made a gutsy call of severing the Russian ties completely, even if it meant a fire sale.

After complex negotiations, VEON sold its Russia unit (Beeline Russia) to local management in October 2023. This was a turning point: the “Russia question” was answered, and VEON could emerge as a pure-play frontier markets operator, no longer straddling sanctions or picking sides. The divestiture massively reduced VEON’s risk profile and leverage. It was like amputating a gangrenous limb to save the patient.

Meanwhile, in its remaining markets (Ukraine, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Bangladesh), VEON doubled down on a strategy to become a “digital operator”. That means not just selling voice and data, but also fintech, entertainment, and other apps to engage users 1,440 minutes a day (their “DO1440” initiative: Digital Operator 1440 minutes ).

It’s similar to what some LatAm telcos did: leverage the telecom base to roll out mobile money, streaming, and other services.

  • Telefónica (Movistar): In markets like Peru, Colombia, and Argentina, Telefónica used its telecom base to expand into Movistar Money (consumer loans), Movistar Play (streaming), and Movistar Cloud (digital storage). These value-added services increased ARPU and customer stickiness much like VEON’s push with JazzCash and Kyivstar TV.

  • América Móvil (Claro): Carlos Slim’s group turned its carrier into a regional ecosystem: Claro Pay in Mexico and Brazil, Claro Video, Claro Música, and Claro Drive all ride on the telco backbone. The logic is identical, monetize the subscriber base through financial and entertainment add-ons.

  • Millicom (Tigo): Tigo pioneered Tigo Money, a mobile wallet in Paraguay and Bolivia that became one of the first large-scale fintech successes in the region. It was built directly on its mobile subscriber infrastructure, echoing VEON’s JazzCash playbook.

VEON’s management also slashed costs (headquarters opex down >50% with a big restructuring) and prepped asset sales to raise cash.

By 2024, VEON was leaner and refocused. It even relocated HQ to Dubai (neutral ground and investor-friendly). Yet the stock was still priced as if disaster was imminent. That’s the “orphan” status: many institutions couldn’t or wouldn’t touch VEON due to lingering Russia/Ukraine overhang.

A Frontier Markets Underdog

Today, VEON operates in five countries (Ukraine, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Bangladesh, Uzbekistan) with 150 million mobile customers.

In most of these, VEON is either #1 or #3 by market share. For instance, it’s the top operator in Ukraine, Pakistan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and #3 in Bangladesh. These are high-growth, youthful markets with a combined population over half a billion people.

Mobile and data services still have room to run. Smartphone penetration is rising and many users have yet to upgrade from basic 2G/3G to 4G. In fact, across VEON’s markets, 4G user penetration ranges roughly 50–70%, leaving a big runway to get remaining users onto higher ARPU data plans. More on that in a bit.

VEON’s history set the stage: It went from a sprawling empire (with even some ventures in Italy, Algeria, etc.) to a focused group of frontier-market ops. It survived war, sanctions, and severed a limb to save the body. Now the market is beginning to see the new VEON for what it is: an unloved telecom that might just transform into a growthy digital services platform.

If you sense my excitement, you’re not wrong. Before I get carried away, let’s break down how VEON makes money today, and why I believe the market is mispricing its future.

How VEON Makes Money: Telco 101 Meets Digital 2.0

VEON’s core business is still mobile telecom services providing voice, data, SMS, and broadband to consumers and businesses. If you’ve ever paid a phone bill, you get the basics. In 2024, the lion’s share of VEON’s ~$3.7B in revenue came from traditional telecom. But the real story is the shifting mix: VEON is aggressively growing its digital services segment on top of that telecom foundation.

Think of VEON as a telco with three interlocked pillars:

Connectivity (Telecom Services)

This is the bread-and-butter of voice minutes, data plans, SMS, and some fixed-line broadband/TV. VEON’s mobile brands compete on network coverage and price. They earn money through prepaid and postpaid plans, data bundles, etc.

Importantly, as more customers move to 4G and consume more data, ARPU tends to rise. VEON notes that upgrading a basic voice user to a 4G “multiplay” user can 3–4x their ARPU. So, a key driver is migrating its large 2G/3G base to 4G. As of Q2 2025, VEON had 103 million 4G users (about 68% of its user base, up from 63% a year prior) .

More 4G = more data usage = more revenue.

Digital Ecosystem

This is the exciting part where VEON differentiates. The company has built or acquired a suite of digital services, often country-specific, to cross-sell to its telecom customers. Examples: JazzCash in Pakistan (a mobile payments and banking app), Toffee or Tamasha in Bangladesh (streaming entertainment), Helsi in Ukraine (a digital healthcare platform), and recently Uklon in Ukraine (a ride-hailing app akin to Uber).

VEON bundles and promotes these services through its apps (e.g., the MyVeon or MyBL app in Bangladesh that integrates health and music). The goal: increase customer engagement (and spending) beyond basic connectivity.

These digital services typically have higher margins than pure connectivity once scale is achieved. For example, fintech transactions or ad revenues can add high-margin income.

In Q2 2025, Direct Digital Revenue was $180M, up a whopping 56.6% y/y. This now accounts for 16.5% of VEON’s total revenues, up from 11.2% a year ago. In other words, the digital side is growing fast and becoming a meaningful chunk of the business.

VEON’s direct digital service revenues jumped from $115 million in Q2 2024 to $180 million in Q2 2025. These high-growth, high-margin digital revenues (fintech, entertainment, ride-hailing, etc.) now contribute 16.5% of total sales, up from 11.2% a year ago.

Asset-Light Infrastructure (Tower & Fiber Leasing)

Historically, telcos own tons of infrastructure from tower masts, fiber cables and data centers. That infrastructure ties up huge amounts of capital. VEON is flipping that model by selling its tower portfolios and leasing capacity instead, freeing up cash for digital expansion.

This isn’t new.

AT&T sold thousands of towers to Crown Castle years ago, Telefónica monetized its towers through Telxius, and América Móvil spun off Sitios Latinoamérica. They all realized those towers were better owned by specialists.

I saw the same story firsthand. One of my mandates at Entel was figuring out how to monetize our tower network. You quickly learn that towers look glamorous on the balance sheet but they eat capital and return little unless you sell them. VEON is following that same playbook, shifting from owning heavy infrastructure to renting it and redeploying capital into higher-margin digital services.

For example, in 2024 VEON sold 2,012 towers in Bangladesh for $100M, and in 2025 it sold its Pakistan towers (+10,500 towers) for $562M. These deals bring immediate cash and remove maintenance costs, while VEON signs long-term leases to rent space on those towers for its antennas.

The strategy is to become “asset-light,” focusing on services rather than owning steel and concrete. VEON’s CEO indicated their towers could fetch $50k–70k each; indeed, the sales so far back that low end ($50k per tower in Bangladesh and Pakistan). Across its countries, about 13k towers remained before recent sales, so there’s potentially $600M in proceeds if they monetize the rest. Infrastructure monetization is a big part of VEON’s plan to reduce debt and fund growth.

Put together, VEON’s revenue model is shifting from a pure telco to a telco-plus-tech hybrid. The core generates cash and provides a massive user base; the digital services drive new growth and higher ARPU; and the asset sales provide cash infusions and opex savings (albeit with lease costs trade-off).

Unit Economics and Key Drivers

Let’s touch on unit economics briefly (I promise to keep it high-level). For a telco, key metrics are ARPU, subscriber growth, churn, and EBITDA margin. In frontier markets like VEON’s, subscriber growth is moderate (many markets are nearing saturation in SIM cards, often >80% penetration), but ARPU growth can be significant as users upgrade to data.

For example, Pakistan’s ARPU might be only ~$2/month (low by global standards), but as more Pakistanis use 4G smartphones and mobile wallets, that could rise. VEON’s multi-play customers (those using multiple services) grew +24% in the last year to 43.3 million, showing success in upselling bundles.

On costs: Frontier/Emerging market telcos can have decent margins, but currency devaluation and inflation are perennial headwinds. VEON’s approach to mitigate that is two-fold: (1) pricing power, they’ve managed to raise prices above inflation in many markets recently , and (2) cost cuts, the HQ cost cut is one example, and selling towers converts capex into a steadier lease expense, reducing volatility (but increasing opex).

In Q2 2025, VEON’s EBITDA margin was 47.8% up from 44.7% a year ago. Management is targeting an additional 300 bps margin expansion over the next 3 years via efficiency gains.

Another driver: Population and GDP growth. VEON’s countries collectively are expected to grow GDP ~4-5% annually and have youthful populations1. More people entering the workforce = more phone subscribers. Unlike saturated Western markets, a frontier telco can grow revenue just by macro tailwinds and new users coming online.

Finally, foreign exchange is a big factor. VEON reports in USD, but earns in local currencies (Pakistani rupee, Bangladeshi taka, Ukrainian hryvnia, etc.). These often depreciate, which hurt past reported results. In 2022–2023, high inflation meant local currency growth was largely offset by FX hits.

But here’s a twist: inflation in these markets is cooling from double-digits to more normal levels , and some currencies (like UAH) have stabilized due to pegs or IMF support. If inflation outpaces FX depreciation going forward, VEON’s local growth will translate better into USD.

In Q2 2025, they showed 11.2% revenue growth in local currency vs 5.9% in USD indicating FX still bit ~5% off the top. That gap could narrow if currencies stabilize. It’s a risk factor (discussed later), but one that might improve from here.

In short, VEON makes money by connecting people and then selling them more than just connectivity. The better it can upsell a Jazz customer to use JazzCash for banking and watch Tamasha videos at night (using a higher data plan), the more revenue per user it gets. And if it can do that without heavy capex (because it sold towers) and without heavy HQ costs, a greater portion of that revenue becomes profit.

Now that we understand the business model, let’s zoom out to the industry context and see how VEON fits into the competitive landscape.

Industry Landscape & Growth Outlook: Frontier Markets, Frontier Opportunities

VEON operates in what I like to call the “last big telco growth markets.” In North America or Western Europe, telecom is a snoozy, low-growth utility business. But in Pakistan, Bangladesh, Uzbekistan, etc., it’s a different story. These markets have young, growing populations and economies that (despite ups and downs) are trending upward.

For example, Pakistan 255 million people, median age under 21;

Bangladesh 176 million, median age 26;

Uzbekistan: 37 million, median age 27.

These demographics are tailwinds for telecom and digital service adoption.

A few broad strokes on industry outlook in VEON’s regions:

Mobile Penetration

In several of VEON’s markets, mobile subscriber penetration is approaching or exceeding 80-90% of the population. However, smartphone and 4G penetration is lower.

This means many folks have basic phones or limited data use. This is an opportunity for upgrade-driven growth.

As cheap Android phones and expanding 4G networks proliferate, millions will become first-time data users. VEON’s own stats highlight this: they set a goal of 70% 4G penetration; many of their markets were around 50-60% in 2022, now pushing towards that goal.

Each incremental 4G user tends to use way more data (think video streaming, social media) than a 2G user. So the industry is in a transition phase from voice to data-centric usage. That drives higher ARPUs and demand for digital services.

GDP and Income Growth

Except for Ukraine, these countries have seen solid GDP growth historically (4-6% annually on average, aside from the pandemic dip).

Rising incomes mean people can spend more on telecom and smartphones. There’s a reason giants like MTN Group or Airtel Africa have been investor favourites. Emerging market telcos can ride a secular wave of new users and higher spending per user. While macro hiccups (hello, Pakistan’s IMF tango) happen, the long-run trend supports telecom sector expansion.

Competition & Regulation

Each country has its own competitive dynamics. Generally, VEON’s ops hold either the #1 or #2 spot, which is enviable. For instance, Kyivstar (Ukraine) leads with 47% market share, Jazz (Pakistan) is #1 with 38% share, Banglalink (#3 in Bangladesh) is smaller (30% share) but catching up, Beeline (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan) are leaders or co-leaders.

Competition comes from the likes of Telenor (in Bangladesh and previously Pakistan), China Mobile (in Pakistan via “Zong”), or local state-backed players. However, given the relatively oligopolistic nature (usually 2-4 players per market), pricing tends to be rational except when a new entrant comes in (not common nowadays) or governments meddle.

Regulatory regimes vary: e.g., Bangladesh has heavy taxes on SIMs and recharges; Pakistan has had some tough times with license fees. But these are part of the business landscape and usually apply to all players equally.

Digital Adoption

Beyond core telecom, the fintech and digital service space is often a blue ocean. In many frontier markets, the telco is best positioned to offer digital wallets to the unbanked or entertainment to a mass audience, because they have the reach and brand.

For example, JazzCash in Pakistan (co-owned with a local bank) is one of the leading mobile wallets, handling PKR 11.7 trillion (~$40B) in transactions over 12 months, +57% y/y! It has 21 million active users.

Similarly, in Bangladesh, mobile financial services are huge (though VEON is a bit behind there compared to a local leader). This industry trend is telcos leveraging their networks to become fintech and content platforms, which can be a game-changer for growth.

Investors have started valuing these digital arms separately (e.g., M-Pesa for Vodacom, or bKash in Bangladesh). We’ll come to valuation, but keep in mind that these aren’t your grandma’s telephone companies; they’re hybrid telecom-fintech beasts in the making.

War and Unrest

It’s impossible to talk industry outlook without acknowledging the elephant in the room: Ukraine is at war (though Kyivstar has impressively remained operational and even grown earnings), and some other markets face political instability (Pakistan has had economic crises and unrest, Bangladesh has currency pressures, etc.).

The telecom industry itself tends to be resilient (people need communication in good times and bad), but things like power outages, infrastructure damage (in Ukraine’s case, from conflict), or government-imposed mobile shutdowns (it happens occasionally during riots/elections) can impact short-term performance.

The encouraging part is that Ukraine’s economy, while hit hard in 2022, is stabilizing and even seeing lower inflation and some growth in 2023-25. And VEON’s Ukrainian business has adapted. They added backup power to towers, etc., to keep services up amid outages. For context, Kyivstar’s revenues were up 25.8% y/y as the situation normalized a bit.

Overall, the industry landscape offers solid growth with frontier volatility. There’s a secular trend of increasing digital connectivity, and VEON’s markets are among the last where double-digit growth in certain segments (like data or fintech) is still happening. VEON’s local currency revenue growth target is 16–19% annually for the next few years. Ambitious, but not impossible if inflation stays moderate and digital services ramp up.

One more thing: Investor perception is part of the landscape. Emerging markets, especially those in the news for wars or IMF bailouts, trade at low multiples for a reason as they carry risk. But that’s also the opportunity if you can find a case where the reality is improving while perception is lagging. I’d argue VEON is exactly that case now: the reality is much better than the outdated perception (war-torn, high-debt, pure telco).

Now, let’s look at how VEON stands out (or doesn’t) against competition and what its edge might be.

Competitive Position & Differentiation: Local Champion with a Digital Twist

VEON’s competitive position can be summed up as “local champion in each market, with a group-wide digital vision.” In the telecom world, scale and market share matter because they confer network effects and cost advantages.

Ukraine (Kyivstar)

Market leader (~47% share), far ahead of #2 (Vodafone Ukraine) and #3 (lifecell). Kyivstar has been the incumbent since the 90s; it’s a beloved brand with deep customer trust.

Despite the war, it maintained service and even increased its subscriber market share. Its differentiation: network quality (it has the widest coverage) and a growing suite of digital services (Kyivstar TV, the Helsi medical platform, and now Uklon ride-hailing integrated).

It’s also now the only pure-play Ukrainian stock listed in the U.S., which gives it visibility. Kyivstar’s margins are very high (EBITDA margin was 58% in Q2 2025 ), indicating an excellent competitive moat.

Pakistan (Jazz)

Co-number 1 in a fiercely competitive market with 4 players. Jazz (VEON’s brand) leads in subscribers and revenue, neck-and-neck with Telenor’s local opco and Zong (China Mobile).

The differentiator here has been JazzCash, which turned Jazz from just another telco into a fintech powerhouse. JazzCash is integral to Pakistan’s digital banking ecosystem. Jazz also has a strong 4G network and brand heritage (Mobilink/Jazz has been around since the 90s).

Pakistan’s macro picture is easing. Inflation spiked into the mid-30s in 2023, then slid to low single digits through 2025.

The rupee stopped free-falling and has been broadly stable since mid-2023. Even in that backdrop, Jazz kept growing double-digit in local currency and held solid EBITDA.

It’s seen as the more innovative player (with music apps, streaming, etc., in addition to fintech).

One competitive advantage:

Scale. With 71.5 million customers, Jazz can spread fixed costs and has negotiating power with suppliers. It’s also part of VEON’s group, which means knowledge transfer (e.g., digital product ideas from Ukraine to Pakistan and vice versa).

Bangladesh (Banglalink)

This is one market where VEON isn’t the top dog. Banglalink is #3 behind Grameenphone (Telenor) and Robi (Axiata). It has a 23% subscriber share.

However, Banglalink punched above its weight in digital. It was the first to launch some digital services and recently sold towers to focus resources. The competition in BD is intense on pricing.

Banglalink’s strategy has been to target urban youth with digital offerings (it has an app “Toffee” which streams content to 4.4M users).

The upside is that if Banglalink can claw its way to #2 or drive higher 4G uptake, it could surprise.

Kazakhstan & Uzbekistan (Beeline)

VEON’s Beeline brand is #1 in Kazakhstan and #2 (close to #1) in Uzbekistan. These are profitable operations with high margins (fewer players in the market, typically just 2-3). They’ve been investing in 4G rollout.

Differentiation: Beeline is known for good network quality and has started digital ventures (like a mobile wallet in UZ, entertainment content in KZ). The competition is often state-affiliated telecoms or smaller players.

Being part of VEON helps. For instance, they can use proven apps or services across markets (a digital education platform launched in Uzbekistan might be ported from something in Pakistan, etc.).

The common thread: in each market, VEON’s opco tends to be either the leader or a strong #2/#3 with ambition, and it’s pushing beyond the basic telco role. This contrasts with some competitors who remain pure-play telcos.

For example, Telenor exited a bunch of these markets (they sold Pakistan operations recently), and others like Airtel or Vodafone in similar markets are still mostly telecom-focused (though Airtel Africa is doing mobile money too).

VEON’s differentiation at the group level is its “digital operator” strategy. This isn’t just corporate buzz; we see it in numbers. Digital monthly active users (MAUs) across VEON’s services reached 119.7 million in June 2025, meaning a huge chunk of the customer base is engaging with at least one digital product.

That builds loyalty (lower churn) and revenue diversification. A Jazz customer using JazzCash is less likely to switch to a rival carrier, for instance. So the digital ecosystem is a competitive moat in the making.

Another edge: Capital allocation and agility. VEON has shown it’s willing to make big moves (selling whole country operations, selling infrastructure, buying back shares) which some state-run or bureaucratic peers might not do.

This shareholder-focused approach is not common in frontier telecoms. Case in point, in 2024 VEON announced a $100M share buyback (when the stock was dirt cheap). They retired 2.14 million ADS (about 3% of float) at $46.55 average.

That signals confidence and improves per-share metrics. Management also paid down a lot of debt with asset sale proceeds, whereas some competitors might have sat on cash or diverted it elsewhere.

In short, VEON is turning its scale into a platform. It’s like the MTN of Eurasia or the América Móvil of these regions, but arguably even more undervalued.

Of course, being good in your neighbourhood doesn’t guarantee stock success; management execution and smart capital allocation do. So let’s talk about who’s at the helm and how they’re steering this ship.

Management & Capital Allocation: Skin in the Game and a Plan in Motion

VEON’s management team has been battle-tested by crisis and appears laser-focused on shareholder value (a refreshing thing to say about a former state-influenced telecom!).

CEO Kaan Terzioğlu

Appointed in 2021, Kaan is a telecom veteran, previously co-CEO of VEON and before that CEO of Turkcell. He’s Turkish, which interestingly positions him culturally between East and West.

Perhaps helpful in navigating VEON’s diverse markets. Under his leadership, VEON executed the Russia exit, accelerated the digital strategy, and initiated asset sales and buybacks.

In his own words, they aim to “deepen customer impact and enhance long-term shareholder value” and so far actions back that up. One telling move: bringing Mike Pompeo (yes, the former US Secretary of State) onto the board of Kyivstar during the war and on the board of VEON, signalling strong alignment with Ukraine and the West.

That’s not a trivial decision; it shows management playing strategic chess to gain trust and perhaps ease investor concerns about governance/sanctions. Terzioğlu has also been very outspoken about the stock’s undervaluation, often highlighting how VEON’s sum-of-parts is multiples of its trading price.

Board and Governance

VEON’s board is an interesting mix. Historically, it had representation from its large shareholders, like LetterOne (a fund linked to Russian investors). However, post-invasion, those ties were cut, and those directors resigned.

Now the board has folks like Gennady Gazin (Ukrainian-American), and as mentioned, Pompeo. The top shareholder today is Lingotto Investment Management LLP, which owns about 8.5% of VEON. It’s backed by Exor N.V., the Agnelli family’s investment arm (Fiat, Ferrari, Juventus). Then you have Shah Capital at around 7%, known for its activist tilt and deep value focus, followed by smaller institutional and quantitative holders like Helikon, Solus, Wellington, and BNP Paribas AM.

Interestingly, the mix isn’t dominated by passive ETFs or sovereign funds. It’s mostly active managers, value funds, and a few quant shops. That’s a healthy setup as these investors care about fundamentals, cash flow, and buybacks. They’re not tagging along because an index tells them to; they’re here because they see upside.

Capital allocation highlights

  • Sold Algeria (Djezzy) stake for $682M in 2022.

  • Sold Russia for $2.2 billion equivalent (though that was mostly to escape liabilities, not a big cash boon).

  • Sold towers in multiple countries, raising >$600M so far (Pakistan $188M received, more to come; Bangladesh $100M; etc.).

  • Reinvested in high-ROI projects: e.g., $600M network spend in Ukraine over 3 years (co-announced with Kyivstar listing) to maintain quality, which should yield returns as they dominate post-war rebuilding.

  • Acquisitions: The Uklon acquisition in 2025 for ~$19M (97% stake) plus assumed obligations (~$100M total) was strategic. It buys growth in digital. They also upped their stake in Helsi (healthtech) to 70%. These aren’t random; they target services that engage users daily, fitting the 1440 strategy.

  • Share Buyback: Completed $100M in buybacks by Aug 2025, which is notable for a company of its size.

The management seems to treat each opco with a private equity mindset: grow it, optionally monetize part of it (like listing Kyivstar, or bringing in partners for others).

For instance, they’re open to local listings or minority stake sales if it unlocks value. The Kyivstar Nasdaq listing is a case in point: instead of keeping 100% of Ukraine in the conglomerate shadow, they spun it out via a SPAC to get a market value. As of now, the market says Kyivstar Group is worth around $2.7 billion (market cap) as a standalone. VEON still holds 89.6%, so roughly $2.4B of value attributable to VEON, equal to 69% of VEON’s entire market cap just for Ukraine!

This kind of capital move is shareholder-friendly; it’s forcing recognition of value that was hidden. (I’ll talk more about Kyivstar’s value in the next section.)

One cannot ignore debt management as a key part of capital allocation, too. VEON had high debt a few years back. Post-Russia sale and tower sales, net debt is around $3.1B (gross $4.9B, cash $1.8B).

They’ve been paying down bonds on time and even got a credit rating from Fitch.

A lower debt load means less risk and potentially the resumption of dividends down the road. VEON suspended dividends in 2020 due to COVID, but historically, they paid quite generous dividends.

Management has hinted that once things stabilize (and once Kyivstar can upstream cash from Ukraine as capital controls ease ), they will consider returning to dividends or more buybacks. The CFO recently noted they upstreamed $59M of dividends from opcos in Q2 2025, a sign that cash is flowing again from subsidiaries (even $15M out of Ukraine, which had been locked, came through after a special permission).

Management is doing almost everything an investor could ask for: cutting costs, selling non-core assets, investing in growth, highlighting hidden value, and aligning themselves with shareholders. Execution risk is always there, but so far they’ve delivered (just look at the 2025 results beating expectations).

Valuation: Sum-of-Parts Tells The True Story

Time to roll up our sleeves and value this thing.

Often, the best way to value a diversified company like VEON is Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP). Value each country/business separately and add them, then adjust for debt, etc.

Lucky for us, VEON’s parts are easier to value now with some market comps (Kyivstar listed, and others with known tower or fintech multiples). I’ve crunched the numbers (with Q2 2025 as the baseline) and here’s what I find:

1. Operating Companies (OpCos): Telecom Services:

First, I removed the EBITDA for Uklon and JazzCash from the Opco, as I will value them separately. Then, I haircut each OpCo’s running EBITDA by 15% to reflect the new lease expense after tower sales. The true hit should land closer to 7–11%, but I’m being conservative.

For EV/EBITDA, I rebuild a fair multiple from the ground up based on each market’s economics. The fair multiple is derived from my own equation ( [EBITDA margin - Capex] x [1 - Tax] / [WACC - g] / EBITDA Margin). I’m not going to prove it here. If you want the proof, read my book.

  • Pakistan (Jazz, ex-JazzCash): EBITDA $426M, at 5.5x EV/EBITDA = EV $3.30B. Pakistan has inflation but also growth.

  • Kazakhstan: EBITDA $378M, at 5.7x and 75% stake (Verny Capital owns the 25%) = EV $1.89B. KZ is relatively stable and profitable, deserving a bit higher multiple.

  • Bangladesh: EBITDA $155M, at 4.4x = EV $0.80B. Lower multiple due to tough competition and currency controls; Bangladesh’s telco market is a bit more challenging.

  • Uzbekistan: EBITDA $86M, at 6.1x = EV $0.62B. UZ has fewer players and good growth, which justifies a higher multiple.

  • Ukraine (Kyivstar): Now for the big one. How to value Kyivstar’s telecom + digital business. One approach is the market: currently VEON’s stake is worth $2.4B. However, the market might be undervaluing it (due to war risk). In a bull case, I’d argue Kyivstar should be worth at least +$3.5B (for context, it did $865M revenue, $518M EBITDA in 2024, so that bull value is 6.7x EBITDA. Not crazy for a dominant operator with 58% margins and post-war recovery upside). We’ll come back to bull scenario.

Now, sum those opco values: Pakistan $3.3B + KZ $1.89B + BD $0.80B + UZ $0.62B + Ukraine $2.40B = $9B.

2. Tower Assets:

VEON is selling most of its towers. I will use the agreed sale prices or management’s indicated range. The CEO’s low-end $50k per tower has proven accurate.

VEON (still consolidated) had about 13k towers left, according to my math. They sold ~10,600 in Pakistan for ~$562M EV (actually, Jazz received $188M cash now and the rest in installments ). They sold 4,000 in Bangladesh for $100M. Let’s assume remaining towers in KZ, UZ, etc. also go for $45–48k each. That implies they still have $600 million of value in their towers portfolio.

So: Pakistan $563M, Bangladesh $100M plus the $600M remaining would equate to $1.263B for all towers. That aligns with the “>$1.2B” management expectation.

After selling, towers will be off books, but VEON will pay lease (which we already accounted for by discounting the EBITDA by 15%.

3. Digital Businesses (Fintech, etc.):

JazzCash (Pakistan fintech): This is a crown jewel. I applied a 11.4x EBITDA multiple on the running EBITDA of $84M, giving $961M EV. That might seem high multiple, but fintechs often go for 15–20x. I’m being moderate.

Uklon (Ride-hailing): Acquired in 2025, Uklon is Ukraine’s Uber equivalent. I applied a 11.6x EBITDA multiple on the running EBITDA of $37M, giving an EV of $420M. Note that the multiple is higher than JazzCash’s due to the higher margin business.

Others: VEON has some other small digital ventures (e.g., content platforms, small startups). I am assigning a castigated multiple of 7.6x on the remaining digital EBITDA of $73M giving us an EV of $541M.

So total EV of digital assets is $1.9B.

4. Sum and Adjustments:

Now, adding opcos ($9B) + Towers ($600M) + Digital assets ($1.9B) gives Enterprise Value $11.56B.

From Enterprise Value, I bridge to equity by subtracting debt and adding cash. Using debt of $4.9B and cash of $1.8B (net debt ~$3.1B), I get an implied equity value of $8.4B. I don’t deduct balance-sheet minorities here because I already netted minorities at the opco level.

There may be small minority stakes in certain digital assets (e.g., ~30% in Helsi), but the details are undisclosed, making precise estimation difficult and given healthcare is < $8M in revenue, any impact is immaterial to the SOTP.

A market cap of $8.4B equates to a fair share price of $122, a 138% upside from current levels.

Why the gap?

The Russia-Ukraine war still hangs over the name. VEON has rerated off the lows, but the stigma hasn’t fully lifted. On headline comps, emerging-market telcos average about 5.4x EV/EBITDA.

VEON screens near the bottom at 3.8x. At my target EV of $11.5B, the implied multiple of 7.2x seems on the high end. But VEON deserves a high multiple because of its hidden assets. As those get monetized, the value should flow to shareholders through buybacks, special and regular dividends, or listing subsidiaries, the way it did in Ukraine. The SOTP captures that optionality; the current multiple does not.

Even if you argue VEON shouldn’t trade above the market’s 5.4x multiple once geopolitical risks fade, that still implies a $79 share price, 54% upside. I see that as a solid margin of safety.

Now, Bull Case: What could lift that $122 to, say, +$140? Two main levers:

  • Higher Kyivstar valuation: If we value 100% of Kyivstar at $3.5B (which is just 6.2x its 2023 EBITDA), that’s about $770M higher than our base assumption ($2.73B). That extra $770M to equity (89.6% of it to VEON) adds about $10 per share (since ~69M shares). So $122 + $10 = $132. If Kyivstar fetched $4B (not impossible if war subsides), add $6.5 per share. Rule of thumb, for every $500M increment on KYIV’s EV, add $6.5 to the target share price.

  • Other uplifts: Perhaps JazzCash gets a higher multiple (say 15x, adding a couple hundred mil), or towers sell at mid-point ($60k each instead of $50k, adding a few hundred mil). These could push another $5-10 per share combined. Also, simply time passing and earnings growing will increase value. If EBITDA grows double-digit next year and we use the same multiples, the EV goes up.

So a Bull Case share price north of $140 is not fantasy; it’s basically assuming the market stops applying a “Ukraine war discount” and values these assets closer to peers. It may also assume improved macro in Pakistan (which could raise multiples there from 5.5x to maybe 6-7x).

The key is unlocking the value. Management is actively doing this via listings and asset sales. Sum-of-parts is becoming sum-of-parts-you-can-see.

For example, now that Kyivstar trades publicly, we can mark-to-market that piece. If KYIV stock goes up (maybe on good earnings or peace prospects), VEON’s stake value rises correspondingly.

Bear Case Valuation

I mark the opcos at 3.0x EBITDA (depressed), set Kyivstar to zero (assume Russia levels Ukraine’s network and capital controls persist), value the towers at $35k per site as a floor, and haircut the digital assets to distressed marks.

The tower floor is conservative: Banglalink sold 2,012 towers for ~$100m ($49.7k/site), and Jazz sold ~10,500 towers for ~$560m ($53k/site). So $35k is a defensible downside anchor. On these inputs, I get $30/share, about 41% downside from today. That’s my “bombs-falling, multiples-compress, assets fire-sale” case.

Risks and the Variant View

No investment is without risks, and VEON certainly has its share (frontier markets are not for the faint of heart).

Risk #1. Geopolitical & War Risk (Ukraine)

Ukraine remains at war, and that’s the biggest variable in the VEON story. A major escalation could hit Kyivstar’s operations or delay value realization there. Capital controls also mean Kyivstar can’t freely send cash to the parent, limiting short-term returns.

That said, the market already prices VEON as if Ukraine were worth almost nothing. Kyivstar keeps proving otherwise. It’s still growing and generating strong margins even in conflict. My take: the downside from war is real, but largely priced in. The upside of any de-escalation or peace would be enormous. This risk is exactly why the stock is still cheap.

Risk #2. Macroeconomic & Currency Risk

Pakistan and Bangladesh are volatile: IMF programs, devaluations, and bouts of high inflation can turn strong local growth into flat USD results. If PKR/BDT slide again, Jazz’s reported numbers could take a hit.

VEON counters with pricing power (regular tariff resets), and the portfolio helps as countries don’t move in lockstep. Ukraine’s hryvnia is also stabilized by a peg for now.

My read: this is standard frontier risk, already reflected in the price. Diversification and active pricing should blunt the blows, and the current valuation gives a wide margin of safety.

Risk #3. Regulatory & Political Intervention

Telecom invites meddling: tariffs, taxes, license fees, new rules. Bangladesh has tweaked tower-sharing and SIM taxes; Pakistan can change fee structures after elections.

That can pinch margins, but outright grabs are rare and usually negotiated. Most of VEON’s countries want foreign capital, so they tend to nudge, not nuke, the operators. VEON mitigates by staying close to regulators and securing practical carve-outs (e.g., power-outage exemptions in Pakistan).

Net-net: expect periodic policy friction, not value destruction. It’s a manageable, priced-in risk.

Risk #4. Execution Risk on Digital Transformation

VEON’s future hinges on digital. If JazzCash loses ground to fintech rivals or Uklon fails to outpace Uber, the story reverts to a slow-growth telco. Critics might call the digital bets money pits, especially with capex spiking during integrations.

But the numbers argue otherwise: digital revenue is up +57% y/y, JazzCash users +19% y/y, and Kyivstar TV dominates its niche. Even if only half succeed, the core business still supports more value than today’s price.

At current levels, digital is basically a free call option.

Risk #5. High Yield and Financing Risk

War-time stress pushed VEON’s yields into junk territory, and maturities land in 2025–2027. That’s the risk. The offset: they’ve already retired near-term notes (about $472M in April and $100M in June) and cut leverage to roughly 1.3x net debt/EBITDA.

Add in tower-sale proceeds and optional stake sales (if needed), plus roughly $600M of LTM FCF, and the refinancing risk looks manageable. In short, funding was the 2022 problem; today, VEON has multiple outs and a balance sheet that can handle the roll.

In essence, the bear case for VEON was already in full swing in 2022: war, collapsing FX, potential default. That bear case clobbered the stock to under $10 at one point. But since then, all except the war risk have been addressed:

  • Russia: ongoing 🙁

  • Debt: reduced.

  • Operations: stable/improving.

  • Management: delivered on promises.

By late 2024, the stock recovered to pre-war levels and is now 34% above that level, but I believe it hasn’t fully shaken off the “icky” perception.

Many investors simply haven’t revisited it, or can’t due to mandates (some funds can’t invest in anything remotely Russia-adjacent, even though it’s not anymore).

Variant View: I see an overlooked transformation where the market is anchoring on yesterday’s fears, while the reality and forward trajectory are much more optimistic. The consensus (to the extent there is any following at all) might be “ehh, risky markets, war, pass.” My view is that these risks are either over-discounted or improving, and that VEON’s unique moves (listing Kyivstar, selling towers, etc.) will force a re-rating.

What to Watch

  • Quarterly earnings (next up Q3 2025 on November 10): look for continued local growth > inflation, and any updated guidance.

  • Kyivstar’s separate reporting (it will file 10-Qs now as a public entity): an interesting peek into one part of VEON. Here is the first released 10-Q.

  • Management commentary on Bangladesh spectrum auctions or Pakistan’s regulatory environment: potential one-off costs could pop up (a risk to watch, e.g., upcoming spectrum renewals).

  • Political changes: e.g., Bangladesh election in late 2025, if it goes smoothly, could ease concerns of unrest.

Final Verdict

VEON is a deep dive case of perception vs. reality. The perception (war-torn, risky, complicated) kept most investors away. The reality is a fundamentally strong collection of telecom franchises pivoting successfully into digital services, led by a savvy management, and trading at a giveaway price. This stock is too damn cheap relative to the quality and prospects of the business.

I see an asymmetric bet, limited downside (thanks to hard assets and essential services even in tough times) and a +130% upside if (when) normalcy returns to its markets. It’s not often you find a company growing revenues double-digit, deleveraging, and buying back shares, yet available at 3.8x EBITDA and 5x forward earnings.

That’s a mispricing of “roadkill” proportions. I’ve seen this movie in LatAm before; those who bought during crises laughed all the way to the bank later.

Could I be wrong? Sure, if war escalates drastically or if multiple economies implode at once, VEON could stagnate or worse. But the margin of safety here (so much bad news already baked in) makes the risk-reward attractive. For adventurous investors who can stomach frontier markets volatility, VEON offers a rare opportunity to own a digital telecom platform on the cheap.

Happy investing and see you in the next issue!
